newsitem.title: USA: Clinton declines, undecideds rise in Reuters poll. [CORRECTED 19:58 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Clinton declines, undecideds rise in Reuters poll. [CORRECTED 19:58 GMT]

text.p: President Bill Clinton's lead over Bob Dole shrank to 9.8 percent in Wednesday's Reuters tracking poll, showing scant gain for the Republican challenger but a growing number of undecided voters.

With less than a week to go before the November 5 election, Clinton pulled 43.1 percent of likely voters in the daily poll, compared with 33.3 percent for Dole, 8.1 percent for the Reform Party's Perot and 13.1 percent undecided.
The gap between Dole and Clinton was 12.6 percent in the Reuters poll released on Tuesday. Clinton lost more than than 2 percentage points (corrects by adding ddropped word lost).
in the intervening time and "undecideds" gained a corresponding amount but Dole picked up only four-tenths of a point.

The Reuters poll, conducted by John Zogby Group International, surveyed 1,200 likely voters over three days, from Sunday through Tuesday, and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.
"What is intriguing is the fact that Dole, of course, is not really moving, but that Clinton is losing points and Perot is gaining," Zogby said.
Another significant trend, Zogby said, was the increase in undecided voters.
"In races where one candidate is losing ground, voters normally spend a night or two in the 'undecided' column before they make their switch," he said.
These latest numbers held little cheer for Dole. Regionally, he was tied only in the South and losing in every other part of the United States.
Only seven of 10 Republicans say they would vote for him, and a bare majority of voters who feel the country is on the "wrong track" would pick Dole.

Clinton has a solid lead among 20-something "Generation X" voters, political moderates, Roman Catholics and most women, although the race could narrow among white women who do not work outside the home, Zogby said.

The race for Congress is still too close to call, with 39.4 percent of voters saying they will vote for the Democratic candidate for Congress in their district, while 36.8 percent say they will pick the Republican.
Republicans are slightly favoured to control both the Senate and the House, by margins of about 3 percentage points in both cases.
